operations.name: limit_function_type_contract.md
operations.content:
---
description: p-limit's declared limitFunction takes a PromiseLike-returning fn and returns a Promise-returning fn with clearQueue
type: project
---
In the p-limit package, `index.d.ts` declares the `limitFunction` public contract as `export function limitFunction<Arguments extends unknown[], ReturnType>(function_: (...arguments_: Arguments) => PromiseLike<ReturnType>, options: Options): ((...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>) & Pick<LimitFunction, 'clearQueue'>;`. This is a type-level contract grounded in the declarations, not a runtime restriction: the input must be PromiseLike-returning, unlike the `LimitFunction` call signature whose parameter accepts `PromiseLike<ReturnType> | ReturnType`; `index.test-d.ts` asserts the narrower limitFunction input with `expectError(limitFunction((_a: string) => 'x', {concurrency: 1}));`. The declared return type exposes only `clearQueue` from `LimitFunction`, and that declaration was unchanged when a later edit converted the wrapper's single `Object.defineProperty(limitedFunction, 'clearQueue', ...)` into `Object.defineProperties(limitedFunction, {clearQueue: {value: limit.clearQueue}, onIdle: {value: () => limit.onIdle()}})`; the limiter object itself also gained an `onIdle` property. So in that working-tree state the runtime wrapper and limiter expose `onIdle` while the types do not: the verification file's `types` log reports `Property onIdle does not exist on type LimitFunction.` and `Property onIdle does not exist on type ((x: number) => Promise<number>) & Pick<LimitFunction, "clearQueue">.`, i.e. that declaration/runtime gap was left unresolved, not fixed. Because the limiter object and the `limitFunction` wrapper carry their members independently of `index.d.ts`, adding a runtime member to either one requires a matching declaration edit for type consumers. `index.js` still builds the wrapper by creating its own limiter and returning `(...arguments_) => limit(() => function_(...arguments_))`. The user asked to remember this inspected limitFunction input/output type contract for future maintenance.

newMemories.name: active_count_includes_reserved_slots.md
newMemories.content:
---
description: p-limit's activeCount counts reserved slots: it increments when a queued job is dequeued, before its function starts
type: project
---
In p-limit's `index.js`, `resumeNext()` performs `activeCount++` and `queue.dequeue().run()` in the same synchronous step, while each queue item's `run` is only the resolver of an internal promise whose `.then(run.bind(undefined, function_, resolve, arguments_))` handler starts the actual job function in a later microtask. Therefore `activeCount` counts reserved slots, not only jobs whose function body has begun: the observed probe printed `after enqueue (sync): [] active 1 pending 1` and `after 5ms: ["running-sync"] active 1 pending 1` with concurrency 1, i.e. the first slot was already counted while no job body had run. A consequence for any work that inspects idleness is that a settling job's `next()` (`activeCount--` then `resumeNext()`) hands the slot straight to a queued item, so reading `activeCount`/`pendingCount` synchronously after the decrement can still be mid-hand-off; the working tree's `onIdle` implementation defers its check with `queueMicrotask(notifyIdle)` for that reason. This timing claim is about the scheduling order traced in the inspected source and the quoted probe output, not a measured performance guarantee.

operations.name: clear_queue_pending_only.md
operations.content:
---
name: clear_queue_pending_only
description: Declared clearQueue() does not cancel promises that are already running
type: project
---
In p-limit, the public declaration of `clearQueue()` says it discards "pending promises that are waiting to run" and adds "Note: This does not cancel promises that are already running." The `rejectOnClear` option is documented as "Reject pending promises with an `AbortError` when `clearQueue()` is called." with "Default: `false`."; in the inspected `index.js`, the enabled branch of `clearQueue()` dequeues each pending item and rejects it with `AbortSignal.abort().reason`. The readme states that when `rejectOnClear` is enabled pending promises are rejected with an `AbortError`, "Otherwise, their promises remain unresolved." The docs recommend enabling `rejectOnClear` if you await the returned promises, for example with `Promise.all`, "so pending tasks do not remain unresolved after `clearQueue()`."

existingMemories.name: clear_queue_pending_only.md
existingMemories.description: Declared clearQueue() does not cancel promises that are already running
existingMemories.content:
---
name: clear_queue_pending_only
description: Declared clearQueue() does not cancel promises that are already running
type: project
---
In p-limit, `clearQueue()` acts only on items still in the internal queue. With `rejectOnClear` not enabled (documented default `false`) it just calls `queue.clear()`, so the discarded pending promises never settle; with `rejectOnClear` enabled it dequeues each pending item and rejects it with `AbortSignal.abort().reason`, i.e. an `AbortError`. It never touches already-running tasks: the public declaration states "Note: This does not cancel promises that are already running." Because the default configuration leaves pending promises unresolved, awaiting them (for example with `Promise.all`) is the case for which `rejectOnClear` is documented as recommended.
